pharm: Thromboxane A2/prostaglandin endoperoxide (TP) receptor antagonist; reduces bronchoconstriction and airway hyper-responsiveness
quick: Take once daily, typically after the evening meal
Use only if benefit outweighs risk
Use with caution; dose adjustment data not established
Contraindicated in severe hepatic failure; caution in liver disease
summary: Seratrodast is an orally active thromboxane A2 (TXA2) receptor antagonist used for the prophylactic management of bronchial asthma. By blocking the TP receptor it inhibits TXA2-mediated bronchoconstriction, vasoconstriction, mucus secretion, and airway hyper-responsiveness. It is a controller medication and is not used to relieve acute asthma attacks. It was approved in Japan in 1997 (Bronica) and is marketed in India (e.g., Seretra, Seradair). Hepatotoxicity, including transaminase elevation, is a recognised concern requiring liver monitoring. It is not FDA-approved.
indications: Prophylactic management of bronchial asthma in adults
Control of chronic asthma symptoms and airway hyper-responsiveness (not for acute bronchospasm)

dosage.t: Once daily, typically after the evening meal
dosage.n: Controller therapy; steady state reached in about 4 to 5 days

dosage.t: Use a rapid-acting bronchodilator for acute symptoms
dosage.n: Seratrodast does not relieve an ongoing attack

admin: Administer orally once daily, generally after the evening meal
Use as a controller (prophylactic) medication, not for acute bronchospasm
Ensure a separate fast-acting reliever inhaler is available for acute attacks
Check baseline liver function and monitor periodically during therapy
Discontinue and evaluate if symptoms or signs of liver injury develop
moa: Seratrodast is a quinone-derivative thromboxane A2 (TXA2) receptor antagonist. It selectively and competitively blocks the thromboxane A2/prostaglandin endoperoxide (TP) receptor on airway smooth muscle and other tissues. This prevents TXA2 from inducing bronchoconstriction, microvascular leakage, mucus secretion, and airway hyper-responsiveness that contribute to asthma. Unlike thromboxane synthase inhibitors, it does not affect platelet thrombus formation, bleeding time, prothrombin time, or activated partial thromboplastin time.

relative: Concurrent drugs that elevate liver enzymes
monitor: Asthma symptom control and lung function

preg: Safety in pregnancy is not established. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus, per the manufacturer's prescribing information.
lact: Use during breastfeeding is generally avoided / contraindicated. If treatment is required, consider discontinuing nursing, taking into account the importance of the drug to the mother.
renal: Specific renal dose adjustment recommendations are not well established. Use with caution in renal impairment and follow regional prescribing information; only about 20% of a dose is excreted in urine.
hepatic: Contraindicated in severe hepatic failure. Use with caution in hepatic impairment because seratrodast is cleared mainly by hepatic biotransformation and can elevate hepatic transaminases. Monitor liver function and discontinue if significant injury occurs.

major: Cephem (cephalosporin) antibiotics (increased risk of liver damage)
moderate: Drugs that can cause hemolytic anemia
Other potentially hepatotoxic agents (additive liver injury risk)
minor: Other anti-inflammatory analgesics (use concurrently with caution)
interactions.food: Commonly taken after the evening meal; food does not preclude administration
interactions.alcohol: Avoid excessive alcohol intake, which adds to hepatic burden in a drug already associated with transaminase elevation
interactions.diagnostics: May increase serum transaminases (AST/ALT); interpret liver tests in this context

emergency: Signs of liver injury (jaundice, dark urine, severe right upper-quadrant pain, marked fatigue) - stop and seek care
Severe hypersensitivity / anaphylaxis - seek emergency care

monitoring: Liver function tests (transaminases) at baseline and periodically during therapy
Asthma symptom control, reliever use, and lung function
Signs and symptoms of hepatic injury
Signs of hypersensitivity or unusual bleeding
counsel: This medicine prevents asthma symptoms; it does not relieve a sudden attack, so always keep your reliever inhaler available
Take it once daily, usually after the evening meal, and do not stop without consulting your doctor
Report yellowing of skin or eyes, dark urine, persistent nausea, or right-sided abdominal pain promptly
Tell your clinician about all other medicines, especially paracetamol and antibiotics
Limit alcohol to reduce additional strain on the liver
pk: Controller effect develops over days; steady state in about 4 to 5 days
Peak plasma concentration about 3 to 4 hours after dosing
Store below 30 C, protected from light and moisture (per product label)
pearls: Not FDA-approved; information is derived from manufacturer prescribing information and regional (Japan/India) sources. The drug was approved in Japan in 1997 (Bronica) and is marketed in India (e.g., Seretra, Seradair). No EMA SmPC or BNF monograph is available for this agent.
It is a prophylactic controller, not a reliever - it will not abort an acute asthma attack
Hepatotoxicity (transaminase elevation) is the key safety concern; monitor liver function and avoid combining with other hepatotoxic drugs such as paracetamol and certain antibiotics
Highly protein bound (over 96%) and cleared mainly by hepatic metabolism; only about 20% is excreted in urine
Does not affect platelet function, bleeding time, PT, or aPTT, distinguishing it from thromboxane synthase inhibitors
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the once-daily schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up.
overdose: Specific overdose data are limited. Manage supportively with monitoring of liver function and cardiovascular status. There is no specific antidote. Seek emergency medical care or contact a poison control center.
